system:
You are the Arabic language reviewer, standing in for an Arabic reviewer at the issuing authority. You compare the Arabic text with the English text and report any difference in meaning: numbers, times, places, the hazard, and above all the protective action. You cannot approve the Arabic; a named person who reads Arabic still must.
You see only the English and Arabic headline, description and instruction, and how the Arabic was produced. You cannot approve or send the alert; people decide.

Review the alert within your mandate only. Decide:
- "agree": nothing within your mandate is wrong;
- "object": something is wrong and the drafter can fix it (say how in `fix`);
- "escalate": something is wrong that needs a decision by a person or a higher authority.

Every objection needs evidence. Each evidence item is a word-for-word quote (at least 5 words for a
clause, at least 3 for the alert or inputs) from either a knowledge base clause shown to you (kind
"clause", ref = its id) or the material you were shown (kind "view", ref = the field name). Quotes are
checked by code; an objection with no quote that matches is thrown away. Do not object to things
outside your mandate. Do not repeat the same issue twice.
If you have a concern but none of the clauses shown supports it, put it in `no_basis` instead.

data.summary: The Arabic headline and description match the English: 19:00, 4 March, under 2,000 metres, northwesterly dust and sand, coastal and inland areas, and the National Centre of Meteorology as source. The instruction does not match. The English tells people no precautions are needed and to drive as normal. The Arabic tells them to take extra care, especially when driving on open roads, and adds a link that is not in the English. These are opposite protective actions. The Arabic advice fits better with visibility under 2,000 m, so the English may be the text that is wrong. A person at the issuing authority must decide which protective action is intended before either version can go out. The Arabic is labelled as machine translation, but its instruction is clearly not a translation of the English. A named Arabic reader must still approve the final text.

objections.issue: The protective action is the opposite in the two languages. English: no precautions, drive as normal. Arabic: exercise extra caution, especially while driving on open roads, because visibility may drop. Arabic readers and English readers would be told to behave differently. The issuer must decide which action is correct; the reviewer cannot pick one.
objections.fix: The issuing authority decides the intended protective action. Given visibility under 2,000 m, the caution in the Arabic may be the intended one; the English should then be revised to say the same. Whichever action is chosen, the other language is redone as a faithful translation of it and checked by a named Arabic reader.

objections.issue: The Arabic instruction adds a reason (visibility may drop because of blowing dust) and an updates link (https://alerts.example.ae). Neither appears in the English instruction, so the two languages give different information.
objections.fix: After the protective action is settled, either add the same reason and link to the English or remove them from the Arabic, so both versions carry identical content.
